content: The noble gases are the elements located in Group 18 of the periodic table, sometimes referred to as Group 0 in the IUPAC system or Group 8. This group is also known as the helium family or neon family. Chemically, noble gases are highly stable because their outer electron shells are completely filled with the maximum number of valence electrons. This stability can be explained through the principles of electronic configuration and quantum mechanics. Due to their full valence shells, noble gases rarely engage in chemical reactions with other elements. Under standard conditions, they exist as odorless, colorless, monatomic gases. Each noble gas has melting and boiling points that are very close to one another, resulting in a narrow temperature range in which they exist as liquids. Noble gases are widely used in various applications, including lighting, welding, and space technology. The seven noble gases are helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon, radon, and oganesson (formerly ununoctium). The term noble gas originates from the German word Edelgas, which was used as early as 1898. This term reflects their extremely low reactivity under normal conditions. While noble gases are sometimes referred to as inert gases, this terminology is not entirely accurate because some of them can participate in chemical reactions under specific conditions. The existence of noble gases was not recognized until the development of the periodic table. In the late 19th century, Lord Rayleigh discovered that nitrogen samples extracted from the air had a different density compared to nitrogen obtained through chemical reactions. Along with William Ramsay, he hypothesized that the nitrogen from the air was associated with another gas, which they identified as argon. This discovery led to the realization that an entire group of gases was missing from the periodic table. Eventually, all noble gases except helium were discovered in the Earth's atmosphere, with argon being the most abundant. Helium, however, was first detected spectroscopically in the Sun in 1868 and was later isolated on Earth in 1895. Under standard conditions, all noble gases exist as monatomic gases. Noble gases have completely filled valence electron shells, which makes them extraordinarily stable. Valence electrons are the outermost electrons of an atom and are typically the only ones involved in chemical bonding. According to atomic theory derived from quantum mechanics and experimental observations, atoms with full valence electron shells are highly stable and do not readily form chemical bonds. As a result, noble gases exhibit extremely low chemical reactivity, and only a few noble gas compounds have been synthesized. No conventional compounds of helium or neon have been prepared, while xenon and krypton have shown some reactivity in laboratory settings. Recently, argon compounds have also been successfully characterized. The lack of reactivity in noble gases is attributed to their complete valence shell, which means they have little tendency to gain or lose electrons. They possess high ionization energies and negligible electronegativities. Additionally, noble gases have very weak interatomic forces of attraction, leading to low melting and boiling points. This is why they remain monatomic gases under normal conditions, even for those with larger atomic masses compared to many elements that are typically solid. One of the most common uses of noble gases in everyday life is in lighting. Argon is frequently used as a safe and inert atmosphere inside filament light bulbs and as an inert environment for synthesizing airand moisture-sensitive compounds, serving as an alternative to nitrogen. Some noble gases emit distinctive colors when used in lighting tubes, such as neon lights. Helium, due to its nonreactivity and lightness compared to flammable hydrogen, is often used in blimps and balloons. Helium and argon are also commonly employed to shield welding arcs and the surrounding base metal from atmospheric contamination during welding. Krypton is used in lasers, which are utilized in medical procedures such as eye surgery. Xenon is used in xenon arc lamps and has anesthetic properties. Noble gases can also be represented using a shorthand notation in electron configuration, known as Noble Gas Notation. For example, the electron configuration of carbon is written as 1s² 2s² 2p², but using Noble Gas Notation, it can be simplified to [He] 2s² 2p². This notation makes identifying elements faster and more efficient compared to writing out the full orbital configuration.
